newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Lamont sees no short-term upturn in trading.
newsitem.headline: Lamont sees no short-term upturn in trading.

text.p: Northern Ireland-based textile firm Lamont Holdings Plc said on Wednesday it did not expect trading conditions to materially improve in the short term and it may be forced to close down its loss-making Shaw Carpets division.
"I do not expect trading conditions to materially improve in the short term," Lamont chairman Paul Vaight said in a results statement.

Lamont Holdings reported a fall in pre-tax profits to 2.1 million stg for the first six months of 1996, from 7.8 million a year ago. Turnover fell 10 percent to 58.9 million mainly due to the fall in linen sales at fabric division Moygashel, it said.

"Losses at Shaw Carpets, which are continuing, should be stopped by the end of the year by which time Moygashel's apparel and furnishing operations will have been reviewed to better reflect anticiptaed market conditions," Vaight said.
"We should therefore be able to move forward in 1997 on a much sounder basis," he said.
Lamont said it had begun talks with the workforce at Shaw Carpets in an attempt to find a solution which eliminated future losses.
"If no other solution can be identified Lamont will be forced to close the business," Vaight said.

He said closure would entail closure costs of around eight million stg, a net cash inflow of around 4.5 million stg including the proceeds from property disposal, and the writing-off of goodwill of 3.5 million in the profit and loss account.
This scenario would be the worst possible result, Vaight stressed, and he said he hoped a more favourable outcome could be achieved.
Lamont said its linen making division, Moygashel, experienced a fall in demand for its products in the first half of 1996 and will not return to profit until 1997.

"The furnishing operation at Moygashel has had a disappointing year in a marketplace which has become increasingly fragmented and competitive. Greater emphasis is now being placed upon our exploitation of the Moygashel brand name in furnshings," Lamont said.
Lamont noted that market demand for linen had stabilised and said it would try to service this level of activity rather than attempt to meet short term peaks in demand.

Lamont said its other carpet-related units had a satisfactory first six months. Northern Ireland Carpets successfully launched a number of new product ranges while BH McCleery benefited from a fall in polymer prices, it said.
In the nonwoven sector, the company said Bonded Fibre Fabric continued to make steady progress but had not achieved "the growth in profits which should be possible".
